newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Human rights report charges Australia with genocide.
newsitem.headline: Human rights report charges Australia with genocide.

text.p: The Australian Human Rights Commission charged the government with genocide on Monday in a report into "Stolen Generation" Aborigines removed from their parents during decades of forced assimilation.
A 700-page report tabled in parliament on Monday contained a litany of physical and sexual abuse of Aborigines based predominately on a policy of white racial superiority.
"The Australian practice of indigenous child removal involved both systematic racial discrimination and genocide as defined by the international law," said the report entitled "Bringing them Home".
"Yet it continued to be practised as official policy long after being clearly prohibited by treaties to which Australia had voluntarily subscribed," the report added.

Tens of thousands of Aboriginal children were forcibly taken from their parents under a government policy of assimilation from the 1880s to the 1960s. Those children are called the "Stolen Generation" or "People of the Bleaching".
Today, thousands of Aborigines face a life of family breakdowns, drug and alcohol abuse, violence and mental anquish directly linked to the policy, the report said.

"All they contributed to our upbringing and future was an unrepairable scar of loneliness, mistrust, hatred and bitterness -- fears that have been with me all my life," Millicent, an Aboriginal woman taken from her parents at the age of four, said in the report.

The rights watchdog said genocide did not necessarily mean the immediate physical destruction of a group or nation and that the forced removal of Aboriginal children was genocidal regardless of the good intentions of welfare groups at the time.
"A state can not excuse itself by claiming that the practice was lawful under its own laws or that its people did not (or do not) share the outrage of the international community," it said.
The report calls for a formal apology by all Australian parliaments, both national and state, as well as churches, police and welfare groups.
"The first step in any compensation and healing for victims of gross violations of human rights must be an acknowledgment of the truth and the delivery of an apology," the report said.
Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Monday issued an unexpected personal apology to the "Stolen Generation".
"I am sorry for the hurt, the trauma, many here today may continue to feel as a consequence of those practices," Howard told an Aboriginal reconciliation conference in Melbourne.
In releasing the report, Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron said he too "felt deep sorrow" for the past ill-treatment of Aborigines.

The report also calls for reparation to be paid to Aborigines for their pain, citing widespread sexual and physical abuse of the "Stolen Generation". It said reparation should include an apology, rehabilitation and monetary compensation.
But Herron reinterated the government's opposition to compensation, saying he "could see no equitable or practical way of paying compensation".
